chapters.title: Chapter 5: Markets and the Wider Economy

lessons.title: Why Markets Rise and Fall: Earnings, Sentiment and Global Events

children.text: Market commentary offers a fresh reason for every move, usually invented after the fact. There is a simpler frame. A share price is only two numbers multiplied together, so any price move must come from one of them, or both. Learn to split the move and market news becomes far less mysterious.

body.caption: Profits are what the business earns. The multiple is what the market is willing to pay for those profits.

body.text: Every market move is either a change in profits or a change in what the market will pay for those profits. The first is business reality. The second is collective mood, and it moves faster and further than profits ever do.

children.text: Splitting a Move Into Its Two Parts

markDefs.definition: A fall in the multiple investors are willing to pay for the same earnings. The business may be unchanged while the stock falls.
A rise in the multiple investors are willing to pay, often driven by improving confidence, falling interest rates or a better growth outlook.

children.text: Take a company whose earnings per share grew a healthy 12% in a year, while its P/E multiple fell from 25 to 20, a 20%
de-rating
. The share price did not rise 12%. It fell about 10%, because 1.12 multiplied by 0.80 is 0.896. The opposite case, a
re-rating
, is how stocks sometimes triple while profits merely double.

stats.label: Who Was Wrong
stats.context: Management delivered; the market simply revised what it would pay

body.title: Now Run It the Other Way
body.prompt: A company's earnings per share rise 15% and its P/E multiple expands 10%. By approximately what percentage does the share price rise, in %?
body.explanation: 1.15 × 1.10 = 1.265, so the price rises about 26.5%. Nearly half of that gain came from the multiple rather than from the business. Multiple expansion is the part that can reverse quickly, which is why stocks that ran up on re-rating fall hardest when sentiment turns.

children.text: What Moves Each Half

body.caption: The Two Engines and Their Drivers
headers: Who Inside a Company Influences It

cells: Demand, pricing power, input costs, interest costs, currency, efficiency, one-off items
Almost everyone: sales, procurement, operations, finance
Interest rates, risk appetite, liquidity, growth expectations, governance perceptions, global flows
Very fast, changing by the hour
Mostly nobody inside the company, beyond disclosure quality and credibility

body.text: This split explains the most demoralising experience in corporate life: a year where every operating metric improved and the share price still fell. The team controlled the engine it could control. The other engine was being driven by interest rates in another country.

body.title: Where a Five-Year Return Actually Came From (Illustrative, % Contribution)

children.text: Over long periods, earnings do most of the work and the multiple contributes less than people assume. Over any single year, the ranking often reverses completely. Both statements are true, and confusing the two time horizons is the root of most bad investing decisions.

body.title: Great Results, Falling Stock
body.question: A company reports 20% profit growth and the stock falls 6% the same day. Which explanation is most likely?
options: The market expected more than 20%, or disliked the guidance and margin commentary
Profit growth never affects share prices
Foreign investors are not allowed to buy after results
body.explanation: Prices reflect expectations formed before the announcement. If analysts expected 25% growth, a 20% print is a disappointment even though it is objectively good. Guidance for the coming quarters, margin trends and management tone often matter more on results day than the reported number itself.

children.text: Five Shocks, and What Happened Next

events.title: The Securities Scam
events.description: A large scam exploiting gaps between banking and securities settlement triggered a sharp fall and led directly to SEBI getting statutory powers. The market took years to regain confidence, and the plumbing was rebuilt afterwards.

events.title: The Technology Bubble Bursts
events.description: Indian technology stocks that had been priced for limitless growth fell catastrophically, some losing the large majority of their value. Several of those businesses were sound, but the multiples paid for them were not.

events.title: The Global Financial Crisis
events.description: Indian indices fell roughly 60% from the January 2008 peak to the March 2009 low, driven by a crisis that began in American mortgage markets. Indian companies had not caused it and could not fix it.

events.title: The Taper Shock
events.description: A signal from the US central bank that it would slow bond buying pulled capital out of emerging markets, hitting Indian equities and the rupee together within weeks.

events.title: The Pandemic Crash
events.description: Indian markets fell roughly 38% in about two months as the pandemic hit, then recovered to their previous peak within months, far faster than almost anyone expected at the bottom.

body.text: Read that timeline carefully. Broad indices have recovered from every one of these episodes, but individual companies frequently did not. Plenty of businesses that dominated the index in 1992 or 2000 are no longer significant, and some no longer exist. Index recovery is not a promise that any particular stock recovers, which matters if a large share of your savings or your ESOPs sits in one company.

body.title: Telling a Sentiment Move From a Fundamental One

columns.label: Probably Sentiment or Flows
points: The whole sector or index moved together on the same day
No company-specific disclosure was made to the exchanges
Global markets moved in the same direction overnight
The rupee and bond yields moved at the same time
Volumes were high across many unrelated stocks

columns.label: Probably Fundamental
points: The stock moved sharply while peers did not
There was a disclosure: results, guidance, a large order, litigation, an auditor or promoter event
The move persisted over weeks rather than reversing in days
Analyst estimates for future earnings were revised after the event
Credit rating or lender behaviour changed as well

body.title: The Four Phases That Keep Repeating

children.text: Cycles differ in their details and rhyme in their sequence:
Cheap and ignored.
After a fall, multiples are low, nobody wants equities, and IPOs are postponed. Future returns are at their best here, which is precisely when participation is lowest.
Recovery on earnings.
Profits improve, prices follow, and the rise is justified by actual business performance. This phase is usually the longest and attracts the least attention.
Re-rating and euphoria.
Multiples expand faster than profits. New investors arrive, IPOs are heavily oversubscribed, and weak businesses raise money easily. The story stops being about earnings.
The de-rating.
Something triggers a reassessment, often rising rates or a fraud coming to light. Multiples compress, and the stocks that rose most on sentiment fall most, while earnings may still be growing.
The practical use of knowing this sequence is modest but real: it stops you from treating the current phase as permanent, in either direction.

body.label: The Honest Summary
body.value: Direction is unpredictable, mechanics are not
body.context: Nobody reliably forecasts the next move, including professionals who do it full time. What you can know is how a move will transmit into borrowing costs, ESOP values, fundraising and demand, which is what this course is for.

body.title: Should We Delay the IPO?
body.scenario: You are on the leadership team of a profitable Indian company that spent eighteen months preparing to list. The business is performing to plan. Over the last two months, the broad market has fallen about 20%, two recent IPOs have listed below their issue price, and your bankers now suggest a valuation roughly 30% below what was discussed earlier. The founders are divided: one wants to list anyway to fund expansion, the other wants to wait a year.
body.prompt: Work through the decision properly. What actually decides this?
body.modelAnswer: Start by separating the two engines. Nothing has changed in the earnings engine; what has changed is the multiple the market is willing to pay, which is a market-wide de-rating rather than a judgement on this business. That reframing matters, but it does not by itself answer the question. Four things decide it. First, why the money is being raised: if the fresh issue funds committed expansion with a defined return, a lower valuation is a cost of dilution to weigh against the return on that investment, whereas if the proceeds are mainly an offer for sale letting early investors exit, there is far less reason to accept a poor price. Second, the alternatives: can the expansion be funded with debt, internal cash flows or a private round instead, and at what total cost, including the covenants and interest that debt brings. Third, the cost of waiting: listing later means the capital arrives later, so quantify what a year's delay costs in lost market share or deferred capacity, and be honest that nobody can promise multiples will be better in a year, because they may be worse. Fourth, readiness and credibility: a company that lists into a weak market and trades below issue price carries that history into every future fundraise, while a withdrawn issue can be relaunched with an updated document at relatively modest incremental cost. My recommendation as a framework, not as a prediction: if the fresh issue component is essential to a committed plan with returns above the cost of the capital, proceed with a right-sized issue, possibly raising less now and returning later. If the issue is largely an exit for existing shareholders, or the expansion can be deferred without strategic damage, wait. What should not decide it is the hope that the market will be higher next year, or the sunk cost of eighteen months of preparation, since neither is a reason and both get cited in rooms like this.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: When investors become willing to pay a lower multiple for the same earnings, the stock has undergone a ___.
body.explanation: A de-rating means the multiple fell. Profits can be rising through the whole episode, which is why a falling share price is not automatic evidence that a business is deteriorating.

body.title: What to Do When the Market Falls Sharply
steps: Check whether the fall was broad or specific to your company, by comparing against a sector index
Look for an actual disclosure on the exchange website before accepting any explanation offered on television
Split the move: did the earnings outlook change, or only the multiple
For your own finances, check how concentrated you are in your employer through salary, ESOPs and any company stock, since all three depend on one business
Resist acting on a single day's move, and if you are being asked for advice by colleagues, point them to their own documents and a registered adviser rather than offering a view
Note what you believed at the bottom of the fall, and revisit it a year later, which is the cheapest way to learn how sentiment works

body.label: BSE: Corporate Announcements
body.description: Every material disclosure a listed company makes is filed here, usually before it is reported anywhere else. When a stock moves sharply, this is the first place to check whether there is an actual company reason.

points: A share price is earnings multiplied by a multiple, so every move comes from one or both of those two numbers
Earnings can grow 12% while the price falls 10%, if the multiple compresses 20%, and nobody has done anything wrong
Earnings move slowly and are reported quarterly, while multiples move by the hour on rates, liquidity and mood
Over long periods earnings do most of the work; over a single year the multiple often dominates
Prices reflect expectations, so good results can still be met with a falling stock
Indian indices have recovered from every major shock since 1992, but individual companies frequently have not
You cannot predict direction, but you can predict transmission: how a move reaches borrowing costs, ESOPs, fundraising and demand
